Questions 1-7

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?

In boxes 1-7 on your answer sheet, write

TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

Questions 8-13

Complete the notes below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Sharks: more than their reputation

  • People often see sharks as mindless [8] machines.
  • However, research suggests this view is wrong. For example:
    • After watching another shark, young lemon sharks learned to bump a [9] with their snouts.
    • They did this in order to be rewarded with [10].
    • Grey reef sharks return to the same reef every day with the same [11].
    • Some Port Jackson sharks are always bold, while others are always [12].
  • Sharks may also have emotions. For example:
    • Some sharks return to the same divers, apparently looking for [13].

Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.

Write the correct number, i-ix, in boxes 14-20 on your answer sheet.

ii   A design that has kept out the weather
iii   A ruler remembered by his people
iv   Older than better-known monuments
v   Uncovered by chance
vi   A disputed modern reconstruction

viii   A carefully planned effect of light
ix   Hidden rooms revealed by new technology

Questions 21-24

Complete the notes below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
The winter solstice at Newgrange

  • Sunlight enters through the roof-box, a small opening above the [21].
  • The light gradually spreads across the [22] of the chamber.
  • The doorway alone could not let the light in, as the passage rises towards the chamber.
  • In 1967, the event was observed by an [23] who was excavating the site.
  • Today, places inside the chamber are allocated by a [24].

B   expertise

G   flexibility
groups.content:
Hybrid working and learning at work

Maria Okonkwo is particularly interested in how [31] is passed on informally from experienced staff to newcomers. At an engineering consultancy, she observed a growing [32] on a written messaging system, and a loss of the [33] that often leads to unexpected ideas. Researchers are now trying to design hybrid arrangements that reduce new employees' feelings of [34].

groups.instruction:
Questions 35-40

Look at the following statements (Questions 35-40) and the list of people below.

Match each statement with the correct person, A, B or C.

NB You may use any letter more than once.

List of People
A   Maria Okonkwo
B   David Lindgren
C   Tomasz Kowalczyk

questions.explanation: Answer: TRUE A 2021 study found that open-ocean sharks and rays ' had fallen by more than 70 per cent since 1970 ' – more than two-thirds.
Answer: FALSE Sharks have cartilage rather than bone, so ' they have no hard structures in which growth rings can be counted '. Scientists dated proteins in the eye lenses instead.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The passage describes a 2019 study of the white shark genome but says nothing about whether other shark genomes had been studied earlier.
Answer: TRUE Genes for repairing DNA ' had evolved in ways that seem to protect its genetic material from harm '.
Answer: FALSE ' The material contains no chemicals and does not kill bacteria '; it only makes it harder for them to form colonies.
Answer: TRUE ' Sharks produce antibodies that are much smaller than those of humans '.
Answer: FALSE The work is at an early stage and ' no treatment based on shark antibodies is yet available to patients '.
Answer: killing 'Sharks ... are often seen as mindless killing machines'.
Answer: target They watched a companion 'bump a plastic target with its snout' and then learned the task.
Answer: fish The target was bumped 'in order to receive a piece of fish '.
Answer: companions Grey reef sharks return 'to the same reef each day with the same companions '.
Answer: shy Some were consistently bold, 'while others were consistently shy '.
Answer: contact Sharks return to the same people, 'apparently seeking contact '.
Answer: iv Newgrange is ' several centuries older than the stone circle at Stonehenge and older, too, than the Great Pyramid '.
Answer: vii ' while most of the stone came from nearby, some of it was brought from much further away ' – quartz from Wicklow and granite from the north.
Answer: ii Grooves channel rainwater away, and ' the chamber has remained completely dry for more than five thousand years '.
Answer: viii At the solstice, ' a narrow beam of light passes through the roof-box ' into the chamber; the roof-box was needed because the passage slopes upwards.
Answer: v Workmen removing stones for building material ' quite by accident, uncovered the entrance to the passage ' in 1699.
Answer: vi O'Kelly had the quartz wall rebuilt, but ' Many archaeologists have since argued that such a wall could not have stood '.
Answer: i ' It was clearly a place for the dead, but many researchers believe it was also a temple '.
Answer: entrance 'Above the entrance is a small rectangular opening, known as the roof-box.'
Answer: floor The beam 'gradually lights up the floor of the chamber'.
Answer: archaeologist It was recorded in 1967 by Michael O'Kelly, 'the archaeologist who led the excavations'.
Answer: lottery 'the few places inside the chamber are given out by a lottery '.

text.en: They lived mainly by hunting and fishing.
They obtained some of their stone from distant places.
They left written records explaining the monument.
They took steps to stop water getting into the chamber.
They used metal tools to decorate the stones.

questions.explanation: Answer: B, D Quartz was carried ' from the Wicklow Mountains, around 70 kilometres to the south ' (B); ' The builders also cut grooves into some of the roof stones to channel rainwater away ' (D). They were farmers (A); the stones were carved with stone tools, as metal was unknown (E); no written records are mentioned and the purpose is uncertain (C).

text.en: the types of company that have adopted hybrid working.
the scale of the change in where people work and its wider effects.
the proportion of workers who would prefer to work from home full-time.
the differences in office use between large and small cities.

questions.explanation: Answer: B Offices are 'less than half full', millions work hybrid, and ' The shift is also changing how organisations function, how workers learn, and what city centres are for. ' No types of company (A), preferences (C) or city sizes (D) are discussed.

text.en: It is becoming less important in modern workplaces.
It can easily be written down and shared online.
It is mainly passed on by managers.
It plays a vital role in keeping organisations running.

questions.explanation: Answer: D ' That kind of knowledge is what keeps organisations working '. It is 'never written down' (B), and it comes from colleagues as well as managers (C).

text.en: senior engineers refusing to take part in video calls
junior engineers solving technical problems without help
junior engineers seeing only the outcome of discussions
senior engineers spending less time on technical problems

questions.explanation: Answer: C Junior engineers were rarely invited to the calls: ' They saw the final solution in a report, but never the reasoning that led to it. '

text.en: argues that city centres will always recover from decline.
shows that zoning laws were a mistake from the start.
compares the effects of remote working with the loss of factories.
illustrates how some cities have successfully adapted to economic change.

questions.explanation: Answer: D ' those that changed their rules and allowed new uses recovered, and some became more attractive than before '. Recovery depended on changing rules, so not 'always' (A).
Answer: B (expertise) Okonkwo is concerned with knowledge 'picked up informally': ' If they aren't sitting near experts, how will they become experts themselves? '
Answer: C (dependence) ' staff came to depend heavily on this system '.
Answer: E (spontaneity) ' Casual conversations, which often lead to unexpected ideas, largely disappeared ', because every question had to be typed and sent to a named person.
Answer: A (isolation) New staff felt 'cut off from their colleagues', and researchers are ' designing hybrid arrangements so that newcomers feel less alone '.
Answer: B (David Lindgren) Lindgren: ' Emptier offices do not mean empty cities. '
Answer: A (Maria Okonkwo) Okonkwo lists lower office costs, wider recruitment and happier, more productive staff.
Answer: C (Tomasz Kowalczyk) ' Just as the railways created the suburbs, and the car created the out-of-town shopping centre , remote working is reshaping the way we live'.
Answer: A (Maria Okonkwo) ' We need to be honest about what we lose, as well as what we gain. '
Answer: B (David Lindgren) Lindgren ' expects people's working patterns to shift at different points in their lives ' – young staff, parents, older workers.
Answer: C (Tomasz Kowalczyk) He wants governments to act now, ' rewriting planning rules so that central districts can include housing, schools and green space '.
